tasks.quote: Number one as a lead single. Eleven times. Number one as an album. Nine. Number one as somebody else's guest. Four. Number one as a mixtape. Three. Number one as a joint album. Two. Number one as a compilation. One.
tasks.takeaway: One rapper's #1 placements break into six independent format categories, each with its own count — not one merged tally.

wouldBeALie: Merging the six figures into one combined 'number ones' total would misstate six separate category records as a single record.

mustBePerceptible: For the first group, 'own' must visibly exceed 'guest'; for the second group, 'guest' must visibly exceed 'own' — the reversal itself must be legible.

mustBeTrue: Each rapper has two values — billions of streams on their own credited songs, and billions as a featured guest.
Group membership is decided purely by which of the two values is larger for that individual, not by fame, genre, or era.
The groups are three and three.
tasks.quote: The ones who carry their own records — Post Malone, forty-nine billion on his own songs against six as a guest. XXXTentacion, thirty-five and six. Kendrick, forty-one and sixteen. And the ones who live on other people's hooks. Ty Dolla $ign, five billion on his own records and twenty-two as a guest. Young Thug, eleven and twenty-one. 21 Savage, sixteen and twenty-three.
tasks.takeaway: Six rappers split into two groups by which of their two numbers is bigger: three whose own-song streams dominate, three whose guest-feature streams dominate.
unstated: The unit (streams vs. certified units) and time window for these billions are not specified in this passage.
wouldBeALie: Ranking all six on one combined-total scale would erase the point, which is about which side of each catalog dominates, not overall size.
Implying one group outranks the other, or that these six are an exhaustive set of every rapper's type, would misstate it.

mustBeTrue: The chart's stated function is limited to counting plays/chart performance, not subjective artistic judgment.
